rows.en: But even in the days of the righteous king Hezekiah the disease was not truly healed. It is true that honor and praise are due to Hezekiah for removing the idols from the land and restoring the Torah to its strength, and he endeavored to raise up its study; he was the man who preserved for the last generation a precious part of the literature of the wisdom of the ancients. At his direction the words of the sages were copied and written in a book. Among the things copied at his direction were the Proverbs of Solomon, or at any rate part of them (Proverbs 25). We also find that in his days genealogical scrolls were written for the use of the chronicles (1 Chronicles 4:41), and all the deeds that he did are faithful witnesses to his effort to keep the religion of Moses on its practical side as well. But the old disease still clung to them. When Hezekiah ascended the throne of the kingdom, the first of his work was to restore to their strength the commandments and statutes that depended on the sacrificial service; he drew the priests very near and placed the charge of religion in their hands (2 Chronicles 31). But the prophet Isaiah, who lacked all confidence in the faithfulness of the priests, could not restrain himself about this, knowing how great was another work that was more necessary, for morality and justice were in a very bad state. Therefore he roused himself and rebuked the men of his generation on this matter: that they drew near to the Lord with their mouth and honored Him with their lips while their heart was far from Him, and their fear of God was a commandment of men learned by rote (ibid. 29).{v1_03_15:1} Therefore we will no longer be astonished at the sight that we see. Since it is clear that religion had different paths among the people under the reign of Hezekiah, who was at any rate righteous in his deeds, how was it possible that the ways of morality were corrupted in the terrible manner that the prophets describe in their rebukes? For indeed it was their light-mindedness in keeping the statutes, their holding to the outward act, and that their fear of God was a commandment of men learned by rote, that did all this. And the priests, and no doubt also the false prophets, strengthened their hand in this worthless thinking, and in their self-deception they thought that by this they had fulfilled their duty in keeping the religion and that it was fitting for them to obtain favor from the Lord; but offhandedly all pure faith was lost, and the words of the prophet came true: "for from the prophets of Jerusalem is profaneness gone forth into all the land" (Jeremiah 23:15). But the prophets of truth, who stood on a high level in the understanding of the statutes, rebuked the men of their generation for their error, early and persistently, and did not cease to dispute with their opponents; and they, with the small remnant that kept the way of the Lord in truth, were the bearers of religion and Torah, to keep it according to its first intention. But we cannot picture to ourselves disputes and opposition of opinions unless we determine that they had different ways in the meaning of the statutes, and this too is not possible unless we say that they were accustomed to the interpretation of the statutes.{v1_03_16:1} But we have also found particular traces that show different ways of understanding the statutes at that time, which differ from their meaning at a later time. And the rule that follows for us from these ways is the same rule that was already found in other and earlier times, namely: that in keeping the statutes they did not care to be strict about their exact form, but changed some form for the need of their hour. Thus it is told of King Hezekiah that in the first year after he came to the throne he kept the Passover, but he did not keep it at its appointed time, only in the second month. And what was the reason for his departing from the statute? Because they could not keep it at its appointed time, for the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently and the people had not gathered to Jerusalem. And who will not understand that the writer here gives the two causes that bring about keeping a second Passover, as written in the Torah: the first, the cause of impurity; and the second, the cause of a distant journey? Now, since this Passover was a second Passover, it is not fitting that a festival of seven days, which is the Feast of Unleavened Bread, should go with it; but it is told explicitly that the children of Israel kept at that time the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days (2 Chronicles 31:21).⚠1 And although we cannot say that this is an explicit contradiction of the law of the Torah, for the law is entirely silent on this, yet it is clear that in the Oral Torah the law was not understood so, for according to it the rule of the second Passover is that leaven and unleavened bread are with it in the house. And it is not to be believed that Hezekiah kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month only as a make-up, because the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread too had not been kept at all that year; for where then did he find a make-up for a festival?⚠2 Besides this there are still in the narratives of the chronicles of the kings of Judah various traces that show us the meanings of some statutes at that time, whether in agreement or in contradiction with their meaning in the Oral Torah; but it is not our aim to point to all the details, and the general matters and the many details recorded so far are enough for us. Let us now pass from this to the time of the prophet Jeremiah, to consider the traces of tradition that were preserved in his prophecies.

1.note: The verse on the seven-day feast is 2 Chronicles 30:21; kept as printed.

2.note: Terse argument; read: a make-up is possible only for a festival kept in its time, so the seven days cannot be explained as a make-up.

rows.en: The spirit of understanding that rests on the words of the prophets who preceded him is also the spirit that stirs⚠1 in the prophecies of Jeremiah. His rebukes are against the abominations of the nations, and especially against the perversity in their deeds: on the one side they acted corruptly, did abominable deeds and served other gods, and on the other side they came and bowed down to the Lord in the house upon which His name is called, and thought that by this they had done their duty (Jeremiah 7:9–10). And in such a people, which halts between two opinions and in which the service of the Lord is joined with the service of other gods, of necessity a right understanding of the faith in one God, as it was intended in the religion of Moses, had not yet taken root. In their error and the straying of their heart they held fast to outward deeds and statutes; they afflicted their souls with fasts and offered burnt offering and meal offering without number (ibid. 14:12), but they did not turn back from any of the sins of man, murder, theft and adultery, and robbing the poor, and they said: "We have not sinned" (ibid. 3:35).⚠2 And Jeremiah could not rebuke them enough for this. He spoke against the sacrificial service when it is not accompanied by the fear of the Lord and the keeping of His word in truth (ibid. 6:19–20), and against the trust in the Temple of the Lord, whose gates they entered without amending their ways to do justice and righteousness (ibid. 7:4–6). And as Isaiah complained that they honored the Lord only with their lips and not so in their heart, so Jeremiah complained before his God, saying: "Thou art near in their mouth, and far from their reins" (ibid. 12:2). And in clear words he says that only understanding and knowledge of the Lord are the purpose of religion and the statutes, and the sacrificial service is nothing but the means to attain this purpose, as is seen from the fact that Israel was not commanded in the wilderness concerning burnt offering and sacrifice, but only to hearken to the voice of the Lord (ibid. 7:21);⚠3 of necessity this is not the essence of the service but only the means. And indeed they did not offer to the Lord sacrifice and meal offering during all the forty years that they walked in the wilderness (Amos 5:25). Yet in his time his opponents were many. Even those who handle the Torah did not rise to such lofty views, and they did not know the Lord (Jeremiah 2:8); both prophet and priest went after gain and dealt falsely (ibid. 6:13). And in his rebuke the prophet thundered against these men who were wise in their own eyes, saying: "How do ye say: We are wise, and the Torah of the Lord is with us? Lo, certainly in vain hath wrought the vain pen of the scribes" (ibid. 8:8). And although today, after the thousands of years that have passed since then, we cannot know what the literature was at which the prophet aimed, this we have seen clearly: that these scribes wrote things touching on the Torah, whether they falsified the written statutes and shaped them according to their wish and purpose, or put into them intentions and meanings that they invented out of their own heart. And against this the prophet said that the pen in the hand of these scribes is a false pen, and it also made their Torah, which they call the Torah of God, false as well. Now how can we imagine such events unless we say that on both sides of the opponents the Torah was interpreted, and each of the sides chose for itself its own way in interpreting the Torah and understanding it? But even though we have seen that the outward service was evil in the eyes of Jeremiah, we will not conclude from this that he rejected the practical statutes; they too were precious in his eyes when they were done for a moral purpose. And we also see that the prophet speaks in scattered places of such statutes and warns about keeping them. And how precious is the mention of these statutes for our purpose, since some of them are statutes that are not found in Scripture, and their foundation is only in the tradition preserved for us through the prophet. Thus, when he rebukes them about keeping the Sabbath, he specifies in particular the warning that they should not carry a burden out of their houses on the Sabbath day (ibid. 18:22).⚠4 This detail is not written in the Torah of Moses nor hinted at in it, but its foundation is in a tradition from mouth to mouth, and it is suited to explain the general rule in the Torah that warns against doing any work, and it teaches us that carrying a burden out of the house is also counted as work. And perhaps this statute is already a widening of the statute of the Torah, and carrying out a burden was not forbidden by it except because it is one of the business of the weekdays, from which it is fitting to refrain, out of our duty to sanctify the Sabbath day. And that this is truly so follows for us from the words of another prophet, who prophesied not long after the time of Jeremiah: that is the exalted prophet who is not known to us by name and whose prophecies were appended to the prophecies of Isaiah. He too speaks of the holiness of the Sabbath and counts resting from pursuing one's business as one of the things necessary to the holiness of the Sabbath, saying: "If thou turn away thy foot because of the Sabbath, from pursuing thy business on My holy day ... and shalt honour it, not doing thy wonted ways, nor pursuing thy business, nor speaking thereof" (Isaiah 58:13). The meaning of these words is close to the meaning of the words of Jeremiah, for the words of both are aimed at refraining on the Sabbath from the business of the weekdays. But [Jeremiah] speaks of bringing the burden into the gates of Jerusalem and of carrying it out of the house, while [this prophet] speaks of "doing ways," in which lies the first hint of the prohibition of Sabbath limits [teḥumin] mentioned in the Talmud. But it is clear from his words that "doing ways" is not the main prohibition; he warns only to turn back the foot because of the Sabbath so as not to pursue business, and therefore his intention is only refraining from going on journeys whose purpose is to pursue business; and accordingly the words of both are equal in their inner intention. And indeed in ancient years they were not strict about walking on the Sabbath from place to place, even if the place to which one went was far, if the going was not to do the business of the weekdays but for the sake of fulfilling a commandment, such as hearing the word of the Lord. This follows for us from the story of the Shunammite woman (1 Kings 4),⚠5 whose husband said to her: "Wherefore wilt thou go to him (to the prophet) today? it is neither new moon nor Sabbath." From this it is seen that it was the custom of the good among the people to go on the Sabbath from their city to the place of the prophet. Jeremiah preserved in his prophecies several more customs that were practiced in Israel; some of them the generations after him held to, and some were lost in the course of time. A notable one among those customs is the custom of mourners for the dead. He describes the turmoil in the land of Judah and the multitude of the slain who will not be buried nor lamented: "neither shall men cut themselves, nor make themselves bald for them; neither shall men break bread for them in mourning, to comfort them for the dead; neither shall men give them the cup of consolation to drink for their father or for their mother" (Jeremiah 16:6–7). From this we learn that in his time they used to cut themselves and make baldness for the dead (Radak), and it is very far-fetched to say that he mentioned also those who acted against the law.{v1_03_18:1} And they used to break bread for the mourner to give him his meal of consolation, and gave him to drink the cup of consolation; and these customs are not hinted at in the Torah. He also preserved for us the custom of the ancients in the manner of acquisitions, to confirm every matter in buying and selling: "men shall buy fields for money" (ibid. 32; and see Kiddushin 26a). And he is the first who mentions acquisition by a deed, which he calls "the deed of purchase." From his words we see what the form of the deed was in ancient days; for when he bought a field from Hanamel his cousin, he said: "So I took the deed of the purchase, both that which was sealed, containing the terms and conditions, and that which was open; and I gave the deed of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah ... in the presence of Hanamel mine uncle's son, and in the presence of the witnesses" [Jeremiah 32:11–12]. From this we understand that on the sealed one were written the terms and conditions, that is, the substance of the deed and its stipulations; but what was written on the open one is not said there, and no doubt the witnesses wrote their signatures on the open one. So too it follows from what is described in another verse (32:44), which says: "and subscribe the deeds, and seal them, and call witnesses"; so what the first verse calls "open" is described here in the words "and call witnesses" (see Bava Batra 160b). And so we learned that the buyer wrote the deed of purchase and signed it, as it says: "And I subscribed the deed, and sealed it" [Jeremiah 32:10] (and see Targum Jonathan, and Kiddushin 9a, and this requires study). Now if we look over the generations of the prophets from the days of Samuel to the days of Jeremiah, we find that from among them all clear traces of their interpretation of the statutes of religion shine forth, whether much or little. And in all these traces we have seen that there is not even one of the prophets who took the words of the statutes literally; on the contrary, all of them as one man proclaimed with all strength that in the practice of the statutes one must go down to the ultimate intention of the Torah. Now we see in this long period of time the first stage of the interpretation [midrash] of the statutes of the Torah, and therefore it is also the first period of the Oral Torah. But with its close its stage and its character are also sealed, for from then on a new stage in the understanding of the statutes of the Torah is revealed and appears before our eyes. But these two stages, the old and the new, did not join one to the other exactly; there was a time of transition between them, which was the bridge that connected the one with the other. This time of transition is the time of the exile, and it will close the first part of our account.

footnotes.en: In Kings it is told that Uzziah became leprous at the end of his days. But Chronicles adds that Uzziah burned incense on the altar of incense, and because of this the priests contended with him, and he was punished for it and struck with leprosy. What is clear in this story is that he really burned incense and the priests contended with him over it, and the writer of the book connected the cause of his leprosy with this, as is the way of this writer always to add things of his own, especially where he wants to magnify the standing of the priests and the Levites, for this is among the purposes of his book.

Isaiah chapter 1 was composed in the days of Ahaz, according to the opinion of De Wette, Gesenius and Rosenmüller, at the time when Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah fought against the kingdom of Judah. In verses 2, 3 and 21 it appears that the prophet complains that they turned their way from good to evil, and during the time of Isaiah's prophecy this was so only in the days of Ahaz. So too "Your country is desolate; your cities are burned with fire" etc. "And the daughter of Zion is left as a booth in a vineyard" etc. [Isaiah 1:7–8] fits the time of Ahaz, in relation to the war of Aram and Israel (2 Kings 16:5), which passed through and swept over all the land of Judah, and they came as far as Jerusalem; no doubt they conquered the other cities, and it is right to say "And the daughter of Zion is left" etc. And in 2 Chronicles 28 it is told that they made a great breach among the people of Judah and carried away captives from it. At that time the Edomites too fought against them and carried away captives, and likewise the Philistines, and in all these wars Ahaz was humbled (ibid. 17, 18). Therefore the prophet's words "Your country is desolate" are right. As for the religious state in the time of Ahaz, it has already been told in the text that he was strict about the act of sacrifice, as is said at length in Kings there; and although in Chronicles (2 Chronicles 29:6) it is told "that they turned away their faces from the habitation of the Lord ... and have not burned incense nor offered burnt offerings in the holy place" [2 Chronicles 29:6–7], we must rely only on the book of Kings, which is the main source. Likewise, what the prophet complains of here, the lack of justice (v. 17) and the violence of the princes (v. 23), the wrong against the orphan and the widow, who are the poor of the people (ibid.), he complains of the same in the prophecy of chapter 3:13, 14, 15. And chapter 3 is without doubt from the time of Ahaz. For the prophet's saying "For they are replenished from the east" etc. (verse 7),⚠1 and all the other verses that speak of idolatry, fit neither the time of Uzziah nor Jotham nor Hezekiah. But in the first years of his reign, when the state of the people was still one of temporal prosperity, in whose wake came the inclination to luxuries and to human pleasures that is described there at length (verses 16, 18–23). In general, all the words said in chapters 2 and 3 are fit to be said only of Ahaz and the state of his time. This is discussed at length in the commentaries on the book of Isaiah by the sage Shadal [S. D. Luzzatto] and by Christian scholars, the best of whom assign this prophecy to the time of Ahaz; see Gesenius, Rosenmüller, Hitzig, Ewald, Knobel.

1.note: The words are Isaiah 2:6, not chapter 3; kept as printed.

footnotes.en: Isaiah prophesied the prophecy in chapter 29 in the days of Hezekiah. For in verse 15 he speaks of those who hide counsel from the Lord and whose works are in the dark, and this is aimed at those who sought to make a covenant with Egypt and to lean on it. For from the time of Ahaz, Judah was a tributary vassal to the king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:5);⚠1 Hezekiah rebelled against him and did not serve him (ibid. 18:7), and it appears that he allied himself with Egypt and leaned on it (ibid. 21). This alliance was evil in Isaiah's eyes (Isaiah 30:1; 31:1), and verse 15 is aimed at it. Especially since the whole prophecy is aimed at the siege that would come soon by the king of Assyria. All the commentators have already explained this prophecy as referring to Hezekiah; see Ibn Ezra, and the commentary of Luzzatto, Gesenius, Drechsler,⚠2 Knobel.

footnotes.en: Isaiah himself described such a dispute between the prophet of truth and the false prophets and the priests, in what he said (Isaiah 28:9–13): "Whom shall one teach knowledge? And whom shall one make to understand the message?" etc. The meaning is that Isaiah described the mockery of the false prophets against him and put these words in their mouth: "Whom shall one teach knowledge" etc., "them that are weaned from the milk" etc.; that is: whom does this prophet (Isaiah) want to teach the Torah of the Lord, as if we were weaned from milk, who do not know and do not understand, that he always wants to teach us and gives "precept by precept, line by line, here a little, there a little"? Their meaning is that the prophet's instruction in the statutes is nothing but an addition to the statute that he gives from his own mind: to every precept he adds a precept, and to every line a line, and in every place he finds occasion to add things from his own mind, here a little and there a little. This was a strange thing to this people, and it seemed to them as if he spoke "with stammering lips and with another tongue" when he told them that by keeping this "precept by precept" and "line by line" they would attain "the rest" and "the refreshing" for their weariness, which in their opinion is not so; therefore they would not listen to the words of the prophet. And on this the prophet concluded: indeed so it will be for them, and the word of the Lord will be to them only "precept by precept," and not truly the word of God, so that they will be punished. And he described the snaring and the breaking that come upon them in consequence of this view, that they think of what is truly the word of the Lord that it is only "precept by precept" that the prophet gives from his own mind, as though they [the precepts] came of his own will and desire.⚠1

1.note: Antecedent of הם unclear; read as the precepts coming from the prophet's own will.

footnotes.en: So Radak wrote in his commentary, because he wanted to cover for the prophet, so that we should not think that the custom of cutting oneself and making baldness for the dead was not evil in his eyes. But one who inquires into antiquities has only to judge by the plain sense and meaning of the deeds set before him. And whoever looks at the prophet's words without partiality will find that the truth is that they used to cut themselves and make baldness for the dead, not because they learned this from the nations, but it was a custom that had taken root among them too from of old. In the Torah we find a warning to the priests "that they shall not make baldness upon their head ... nor make any cuttings in their flesh" (Leviticus 21:5), and according to the masters of the Talmud this is not about the dead (Sifra, Emor 1); and of Israel it is only said: "Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead" (ibid. 19:28). Whether cutting and gashing are one or different in their concept we do not know, but at any rate they are close. Gashing was the practice of the priests of Baal and his worshippers (1 Kings 18:28), and in the opinion of the masters of the Talmud gashing was only a scraping of the skin on the surface, for they said that gashing is possible both by hand and with an instrument (Makkot 23a),⚠1 and by hand one cannot make a deep wound in the flesh. Indeed, in Deuteronomy the Israelites too were warned not to cut themselves nor make baldness for the dead (Deuteronomy 14:1), and the reason is given there: "For thou art a holy people unto the Lord thy God," so that it is fitting for you to conduct yourself in the measure of holiness like the priests (and see the next chapter). But in the days of Jeremiah they did not practice so, and this statute had not taken root in the nation. Therefore the prophet too speaks of making baldness and gashing for the dead as if it were a custom of Israel. And even the good among them did so, as is seen from the men who came from Samaria and Shiloh to bring meal offering and frankincense to the house of the Lord: when they heard of the destruction they shaved their beards, rent their clothes and cut themselves (Jeremiah 41:5).

1.note: The ruling on gashing by hand or instrument is Makkot 21a; kept as printed.
